analysis.title: The Oil Squeeze Nobody Is Pricing
key_insights: Oil is holding the rising trend line in place since the July lows. A close above the mid-September closing high near $108.5 would open the door to an upside squeeze.
Implied volatility on oil is depressed even as price approaches recent highs. The market is pricing downside risk and very little upside volatility, so upside optionality is described as cheap.

JPMorgan notes the cost of shipping crude from the Middle East to China has risen to about $35 per barrel from about $3 earlier this year. Delivered Middle Eastern crude now costs Chinese buyers around $143 per barrel.

The current squeeze is about the cost of moving oil, unlike April, when the problem was a physical shortage. Energy importers face a larger cost shock than benchmark crude suggests, and European refining margins are under pressure.
The oil-Treasury yield relationship has loosened recently. Another leg higher in crude could revive inflation concerns and push yields up when rates are already elevated.
US 10-year breakevens have risen recently but remain contained over a longer window. The bond market shows little concern about oil-driven inflation risk for now.

India is described as one of the equity markets most vulnerable to higher oil because of its reliance on imported crude. Higher oil feeds the import bill, inflation expectations, currency pressure and equity valuations.

Korea is exposed to imported energy costs and KOSPI is a concentrated expression of the AI trade. Korean semiconductors are already under pressure, and higher crude could add to the squeeze and raise the question of spillover into the broader AI complex.

Goldman flags significant CTA downside convexity in oil, but the expected selling has repeatedly failed to appear while crude keeps grinding higher. The note questions whether systematic positioning is disconnected from price action.
